title: How Asia’s Surpluses Are Evolving
text:
How Asia’s Surpluses Are Evolving

Udith Sikand

Gavekal Research | 2 Oct 2026

The economies of Northeast Asia all run large structural current account surpluses greater than 3% of their GDP (or greater than 17% in the case of Taiwan). According to conventional economic wisdom, this means their currencies should be appreciating. Yet by any standard measure the currencies of Northeast Asia are deeply undervalued, and if anything their structural trend over the last few years appears to be towards more depreciation. Why is this?Historically, analysts have viewed the impact of current account balances on exchange rates through the prism of trade balances. The current account surpluses of Northeast Asian economies reflected their ability to sell more goods to foreigners than they bought from overseas. In theory, the inflow of export revenues—largely denominated in US dollars—should have put upward pressure on their currencies. But for the most part these economies recycled their excess US dollar earnings into purchasing foreign assets—primarily denominated in US dollars. This recycling kept their currencies undervalued, so perpetuating the whole cycle.
